speaker: April Dunford
title: How to nail your product positioning | April Dunford (Obviously Awesome)
question: In B2B software deals involving five to seven stakeholders, how does the actual buying sequence affect which buyer personas matter for product positioning?
guest: In a typical B2B enterprise software purchase, five to seven people are involved in the decision—the sales ops manager researching tools, end users, IT checking security and integrations, purchasing, legal, and the executive who signs the check. Where marketing teams go off the rails is building stereotype one-pager personas for all of them and treating them equally. Think about how the deal actually happens. A VP tells someone, "Go figure it out." That person does the research, builds the shortlist, takes the sales calls, and narrows down the options before bringing in anyone else. By far the most important persona is that internal champion, whose job is to build consensus across everyone else, including the economic buyer. If our positioning doesn't resonate with that champion, we're dead in the water—we don't even make the shortlist, so we never get to care about the other personas because the champion is the gatekeeper. Positioning has to crush it with the champion first. Then later in the deal cycle, our job is to arm that champion to sell IT, purchasing, end users, and their boss, because the champion is doing the heavy lifting internally.

points.core: One internal champion acts as the gatekeeper who builds the vendor shortlist.
points.note: Accept: a single point person researches options, runs early vendor calls, and filters who makes the shortlist before other stakeholders enter. Do not credit: generic descriptions of buying committees without identifying the champion's sequential gatekeeping role.

points.core: Failing to resonate with the champion eliminates you before other personas matter.
points.note: Accept: positioning must win the champion first or the company never reaches IT, legal, procurement, or the economic buyer. Do not credit: vague advice to personalize messaging for every stakeholder.

points.core: Vendors win secondary stakeholders later by arming the champion to sell internally.
points.note: Accept: rather than treating all stakeholder personas equally upfront, equip the champion later in the cycle to persuade IT, procurement, end users, and the economic buyer. Do not credit: suggesting separate homepage positioning for IT, legal, and purchasing.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The buying sequence matters because stakeholders don't weigh in simultaneously; they enter at different stages with different powers, so positioning has to serve whoever controls each gate rather than an averaged "buyer."

Typically a champion (often a user or team lead feeling the pain) triggers the search and builds the shortlist. Positioning must first win this person: clear problem framing, differentiation, and material they can reuse internally, since most of the deal happens in rooms the vendor isn't in. Next, the economic buyer decides whether the problem is worth funding at all, so the positioning must translate into business outcomes and a case against doing nothing, which is the most common competitor. Late-stage participants such as IT, security, legal and procurement rarely choose you but can veto you; they need risk reduction, not persuasion.

The practical implication: build core positioning around the champion and economic buyer, treat late-stage reviewers as objections to pre-empt, and map personas by role in the sequence (initiator, decider, blocker) rather than job title. Sequence varies by company, so validate it with win/loss interviews rather than assuming.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: In five-to-seven-stakeholder B2B deals, buyers enter sequentially rather than simultaneously, making product positioning a relay race rather than a single pitch. Early discovery and shortlisting are usually led by practitioners or functional managers solving an immediate operational problem, not executives. Positioning that leads purely with abstract C-suite ROI fails here because early evaluators filter vendors by category clarity, workflow fit, and day-to-day utility. Once a vendor makes the shortlist, that early evaluator becomes the internal champion who must advocate for the product behind closed doors. Mid-stage positioning must therefore be simple and portable enough for the champion to repeat accurately while preempting objections from technical gatekeepers in IT, security, and operations. Economic buyers and procurement typically arrive last, wielding veto power over budget, strategic alignment, and payback period rather than comparing features. Consequently, the buying sequence dictates that primary positioning must anchor on the early champion’s acute pain to earn entry, while embedding credible business outcomes and risk reduction that survive internal handoffs to late-stage executive signers.

noweb.answer: In multi-stakeholder B2B software deals, influence is sequential rather than simultaneous, meaning product positioning must prioritize whoever controls entry to the next stage rather than just who signs the final contract. Companies often over-index their primary positioning on the economic buyer, yet executives rarely discover or shortlist tools themselves. If positioning fails to hook early-stage initiators—typically practitioners or functional leads feeling acute operational pain—the product is filtered out before budget holders ever hear its name. Once a tool is shortlisted, however, purely tactical positioning stalls. Because sellers rarely get direct, equal airtime with all five to seven stakeholders, the internal champion must carry your message into rooms you cannot enter. Effective positioning therefore bridges the buying sequence: front-door messaging anchors on concrete workflow value to win practitioners and mobilize a champion, while simultaneously equipping that champion with a portable, executive-ready narrative—centered on strategic outcomes, integration fit, and risk reduction—that survives scrutiny when technical gatekeepers, security reviewers, and finance leaders enter later chiefly to validate or veto the deal.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
In multi-stakeholder deals, the person who matters most for positioning is usually whoever frames the problem first, not whoever has the most senior title. Gartner's research describes B2B buying as a loop of overlapping jobs rather than a straight line: identifying the problem, exploring solutions, building requirements and choosing a supplier. Much of it happens before any vendor is involved.

Early on, a champion or practitioner names the problem and drafts the evaluation criteria. Your positioning has to fit their language and pain, because the shortlist depends on those criteria. In the middle, technical evaluators and adjacent teams such as IT and security act as gatekeepers. They seldom pick the winner, but they can rule you out, so the message to them is about lowering risk and fitting in. Late in the deal, the economic buyer, procurement, finance and legal mostly decide whether it happens and when. They need business-case proof that the champion can carry into rooms you won't be in.

So you should position primarily for the people who frame the problem and the champion, and give the champion material aimed at the later personas. A message built mainly for the executive sponsor tends to arrive after the criteria that decide the deal have already been set.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
In complex B2B software deals, stakeholders rarely evaluate a product simultaneously; they enter in sequence as initiators, evaluators, and approvers. Because of this, product positioning should not try to appeal equally to all five to seven personas. Instead, core positioning must prioritize the early buyers, typically the functional leader or internal champion who feels the acute pain, frames the problem, and builds the shortlist. If your positioning fails to establish clear differentiation and value for this initial buyer, you never make it into the deal.

Downstream stakeholders such as IT, security, finance, procurement, and executive sponsors usually enter after the shortlist is formed. Rather than choosing the product category, they act as validators or veto players focused on risk, integration, compliance, and financial return. Cramming their concerns into your core positioning dilutes your message. Strong positioning wins the champion first, while targeted sales enablement and supporting messaging address each subsequent stakeholder's objections when they enter the process.

noweb.answer:
In a multi-stakeholder B2B deal, the buying sequence dictates that product positioning cannot treat all five to seven personas equally or speak to them all at once. Instead, positioning must mirror when each stakeholder enters the process and which gate they control. Early on, practitioners or operational champions typically initiate the search and build the shortlist; if your core positioning fails to resonate with their immediate workflow pain, you never earn consideration. As the deal advances, technical evaluators, IT, and security teams enter to scrutinize integration, scalability, and risk, shifting what matters from promise to proof. Finally, economic buyers, finance, and procurement step in to validate ROI, total cost of ownership, and business impact.

Optimizing top-level positioning for late-stage executives often starves deals of early champion momentum, while ignoring downstream gatekeepers causes shortlisted opportunities to stall. Effective positioning therefore leads with the initiating persona to win entry, while arming that champion with modular proof points tailored to the technical and financial blockers who arrive later.

noweb.answer:
In a B2B software deal with five to seven stakeholders, the buying sequence tells you whose attention you need to earn first and what each person needs to move the deal forward. Lead with the problem and outcome that matter to the person who starts the evaluation and can champion it internally. Then give that champion a story they can carry to the rest of the group.

As others join, keep the core positioning consistent and change the proof. Users may need to see how the software fits their workflow, IT and security may need evidence that it meets their requirements, and the budget owner may need a business case. If the budget owner starts the search, lead with the business outcome and bring in workflow evidence during evaluation. A stakeholder who joins late can still block the deal, so their concerns matter even if they don’t shape the opening message.

Five to seven stakeholders may weigh in, but they rarely enter the deal at the same time or answer the same question. Positioning should start with whoever frames the problem and shapes the shortlist. If an operations lead starts the search, lead with the workflow problem they need to solve and give them a business case they can take to the executive sponsor. If the CFO initiates a cost-cutting effort, savings may need to lead from the outset.

Later stakeholders matter according to what they can change. Security may need evidence before it will approve a vendor, and end users may determine whether a pilot succeeds. If security sets the shortlist, its criteria belong in the opening message. If it reviews an already preferred vendor, those same criteria can be addressed during validation. Trace recent deals to see who starts the search, who shapes the choice, and whose approval is decisive. That sequence tells you which persona to lead with and what the others need to hear.
